clue.text: Cape Town doctor's Aegean isle?

parts.note: Cape Town stands for its country, South Africa, abbreviated SA
a doctor is an MO (medical officer), here with the possessive S

explanation.surface: A question about which Greek island a South African physician comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cape Town' looks like a place to visit, but it stands for its country, South Africa, giving SA; MO is the usual crossword abbreviation for a doctor (medical officer).
explanation.definitionFit: Samos is a Greek island in the eastern Aegean Sea.

clue.text: A man no longer fresh

parts.note: read as a student who has finished the first, or freshman, year: no longer a fresher

explanation.surface: A man who has lost his youthful vigour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fresh' suggests vigour, but it points to 'freshman', a first-year student; the man no longer fresh is in his second year.
explanation.definitionFit: In American colleges a second-year student, who has left freshman status behind, carries this title.

clue.text: Put down-a point up to the journalists

parts.note: S, south, is a point of the compass
taken as written
the press is journalists collectively

explanation.surface: Someone raises a matter with reporters, only to have it quashed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a' and 'to the' are joining words; S is a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: To suppress a revolt is to crush or quell it.

clue.text: Arrest officer at end of board meeting

parts.note: to arrest progress is to check it
a mate is an officer on a merchant ship

explanation.surface: A company director is detained when the board meeting closes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'board meeting' suggests a company, but the board is a chessboard and the meeting is a game, which ends with this.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess, the move that traps the king finishes the game played on the board.

clue.text: Fratricide can get one put inside

indicators.note: one piece is placed within the other, so the word can is opened to take a letter

parts.note: one is I, the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A brother-killer can end up imprisoned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put inside' sounds like prison, but signals I (one) going inside CAN.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis, Cain murdered his brother Abel, the first killing of a sibling.

clue.text: Raising prices darling ?

definitions.meaning: read as ..., the act of making things dear or expensive
a pet name, a term of affection

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper puts up prices and calls the customer sweetheart.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense splits the word as EN-DEAR-MENT, making something dear; the question mark flags that coinage.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: making dearer, and an affectionate word such as 'love' used to address someone.

clue.text: One pound keep the change that's' the spirit

indicators.note: change tells us to alter the order of the letters gathered so far

parts.note: one is I, the Roman numeral
L is the abbreviation for pound (libra)

explanation.surface: A tipper hands over a pound and says keep the change, praising the generous spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keep the change' reads as a tipper's phrase, but 'keep' is fodder and 'the change' rearranges I, L and KEEP.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scottish folklore a kelpie is a water spirit that takes the form of a horse.

clue.text: Similar way to arrange a loan. Go to America

indicators.note: to arrange the words a loan is to put their letters in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
US is the United States of America

explanation.surface: Advice that the way to get a loan is to go to America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'way to' is a joining phrase; 'arrange' reorders A LOAN to give ANALO.
explanation.definitionFit: Analogous things are comparable or alike in some respect.

clue.text: Some angel, and some brute

indicators.note: some of the words angel and supplies the letters, running across them

explanation.surface: Some people are angels and some are brutes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' signals a run of letters inside 'angel, and'.
explanation.definitionFit: An eland is a large African antelope, a beast or animal.

clue.text: Popular German song about a Pole in full armour

indicators.note: about means going round, so one word surrounds the letters that follow

parts.note: pop is short for popular
N, north, is a pole
a Lied is a German art song

explanation.surface: A hit German song tells of a Polish knight in armour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' suggests a Polish person, but is the North Pole, N; POP goes 'about' A and N.
explanation.definitionFit: Panoply is a complete suit of armour, so someone so equipped is fully armed.

clue.text: A wood-joiner turns into a jungle climber

indicators.note: turns means the word for the joiner is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: a nail joins pieces of wood

explanation.surface: A carpenter changes career and becomes a jungle explorer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wood-joiner' sounds like a carpenter, but it is a NAIL, which 'turns' to LIAN before the A.
explanation.definitionFit: A liana is a woody vine that climbs up trees in tropical forests.

clue.text: Solar System mechanized (not the Waxworks Chamber, 'arry !)

definitions.text: Solar System mechanized (not the Waxworks Chamber, 'arry !)

parts.words: Solar System mechanized (not the Waxworks Chamber, 'arry !)
parts.note: a clockwork model of the planets, which a Cockney such as 'Arry, dropping his aitches, might confuse with the Chamber of Horrors at Madame Tussaud's

explanation.surface: Someone corrects 'Arry, who has mixed up a planetarium model with a waxworks horror room.
explanation.walkthrough: Madame Tussaud's waxworks in London has a Chamber of Horrors; 'Arry, dropping his H, would say ''orror-y', which sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An orrery is a mechanical model showing the planets moving round the Sun.

clue.text: Floral name for that bird in a gilded cage?

definitions.text: Floral name for that bird in a gilded cage?

parts.words: Floral name for that bird in a gilded cage?
parts.note: the bird (girl) of the old song 'A Bird in a Gilded Cage' might be called Mary, surrounded by gold, and a flower is named so

explanation.surface: A question about what flower name to give a caged bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bird' is old slang for a woman; the woman in a gilded cage is a Mary in gold, which is also a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: The marigold is a common orange or yellow garden flower.

clue.text: It's nice, pat, though oddly parrot-like

indicators.note: oddly means in a strange way, telling us to rearrange the letters of the phrase

explanation.surface: Someone praises a pat answer, though it sounds like a parrot repeating words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'though' is a joining word; 'oddly' rearranges IT'S NICE PAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Psittacine means of or like the parrot family, from Greek psittakos, parrot.

clue.text: Writers in Old English, have identical key words

indicators.note: in places the writers inside the abbreviation for the old language

parts.note: pens are writing implements
identical means the same

explanation.surface: Authors writing in Anglo-Saxon share the same key terms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writers' look like authors but are PENS; 'key words' are words that open a door, as in Ali Baba.
explanation.definitionFit: In the tale of Ali Baba, the magic phrase opens the robbers' cave, acting as a spoken key.

clue.text: Cook's vessel-try naming it

definitions.meaning: Captain James Cook's ship on his first voyage

explanation.surface: A chef's pot is given a name after much effort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cook' suggests a chef, but it is Captain James Cook, the explorer; 'naming it' links the verb sense to the ship's name.
explanation.definitionFit: HMS Endeavour carried Cook to the Pacific, and as a verb the word means to attempt hard.

clue.text: Secure stable doors before inmates do so

definitions.meaning: to fasten doors shut with a sliding bar
the horses inside might run off suddenly

explanation.surface: Advice to lock the stable before the horses escape.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb says it is too late to lock the stable door after the horse has run; the answer means both fastening and running.
explanation.definitionFit: To bolt is both to fasten with a bar and to run away suddenly, as a horse does.

clue.text: Army members may have some suckers

definitions.text: Army members may have some suckers

parts.words: Army members may have some suckers
parts.note: army read as arm-y, so the members are arms of a creature like an octopus, lined with suckers

explanation.surface: Soldiers may include some gullible people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suckers' sounds like dupes among soldiers, but 'Army' means having many arms, and those limbs carry suckers.
explanation.definitionFit: An octopus or squid has long flexible limbs with suction pads for gripping.

clue.text: Liable to mimicry, I am able to get round it

indicators.note: to get round something is to encircle it, so the first phrase goes round the next word

parts.note: I am contracts to I'M, then able as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone claims they can get round anyone who would copy them.
explanation.walkthrough: I'M ABLE goes round IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that can be copied is open to being mimicked.

clue.text: Icelandic tales of the restless dead

indicators.note: restless means not keeping still, so the letters of dead are moved about

explanation.surface: Old Norse stories about ghosts who cannot rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of the' is a joining phrase; 'restless' rearranges DEAD.
explanation.definitionFit: The Eddas are medieval Icelandic collections of Norse myth and poetry.

clue.text: The way one Scotsman gets about as a crafty type

parts.note: ST is short for street, a way
taken as written

indicators.note: to get about something is to surround it, so the Scotsman encloses the next word

parts.note: mon is Scots dialect for man
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Scot is described as wandering about like a cunning character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crafty' suggests cunning, but means skilled in a craft; MON (Scots for man) goes round AS.
explanation.definitionFit: A mason practises the craft of cutting and laying stone, and Freemasons speak of 'the Craft'.

clue.text: Edward is willing to see inventor

parts.note: Ed is short for Edward
taken as written
on means willing, as in 'I'm on'

explanation.surface: Edward agrees to visit an inventor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to see' is a joining phrase; ON for willing is as in 'are you on for it?'.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Edison invented the phonograph and developed the electric light bulb.

clue.text: Quietly hastened to get face appropriate for dinner

parts.note: P, piano, is the musical direction for quietly
ran means hastened
dial is slang for face

explanation.surface: Someone hurries quietly to put on a suitable face for dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get' is a joining phrase; DIAL is British slang for a face.
explanation.definitionFit: Prandial means relating to a meal, especially dinner, as in 'after-dinner' speeches.

clue.text: Chooses a box at the Mint, say

indicators.note: say tells us the word for the box is spoken, and another word sounds the same

parts.note: a pyx is the box in which sample coins are kept at the Royal Mint for testing

explanation.surface: Someone selects a box at the Mint.
explanation.walkthrough: At the Royal Mint, the Trial of the Pyx tests coins kept in a box called a pyx.
explanation.definitionFit: To pick is to choose or select.

clue.text: Bloody spot's a disgrace!

definitions.meaning: a mark of bleeding, like the wounds of Christ on a saint

explanation.surface: Someone curses a stain as a disgrace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloody' looks like an oath, but describes a spot that bleeds, as in the stigmata of saints.
explanation.definitionFit: Stigma means both a bleeding mark on the skin and a mark of shame.

clue.text: Figure's all-round figure

parts.note: the number measured all round a body, its waist measurement

explanation.surface: A person's figure is good all round.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'figure' is a body, the second a number: the measurement round the body.
explanation.definitionFit: Girth is the measurement round the middle of a person or thing.

clue.text: Novel plan for a bit of land

definitions.meaning: a small piece of ground, as for a garden

explanation.surface: A new scheme for a small piece of land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like 'new', but it is a book, whose plan is its storyline.
explanation.definitionFit: A plot is both a story's scheme and a small piece of land.

clue.text: Nothing stops one such making three in a row

definitions.text: Nothing stops one such making three in a row

parts.words: Nothing stops one such making three in a row
parts.note: in noughts and ... a nought, nothing, blocks the other player's mark from completing a line

explanation.surface: Nothing can prevent someone winning three times running.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing' reads as 'no thing', but is a nought: in noughts and crosses (tic-tac-toe) a nought blocks a line of three.
explanation.definitionFit: The X mark in noughts and crosses is the other player's symbol.

clue.text: The Italian party member appears close-fisted

parts.note: il is Italian for the
a Liberal is a member of the Liberal Party

explanation.surface: An Italian politician turns out to be stingy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appears' is a joining word; IL is 'the' in Italian.
explanation.definitionFit: Illiberal once meant mean or ungenerous, as well as narrow-minded.

clue.text: It's rigorous being sent out of town in Herts

indicators.note: sent placed out of the town means its letters lie outside it

parts.note: Tring is a town in Hertfordshire

explanation.surface: A strict regime sends someone away from a Hertfordshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Herts is Hertfordshire, a county north of London; Tring is a town there, and SENT goes 'out of' it.
explanation.definitionFit: Stringent rules are strict and demanding.
